body:
Ran a handful of benchmarks to compare, since I suspected it would barely matter for int arrays and so I might as well remove the copy.
The tests below were run in chunks that were interleaved to try to mitigate variance over time.

```
Benchmarked with and without extra copy
                                                 With vs Without
Node sorting:
Array size: 10,     Time to sort 20M elements:  74.2s vs  70.4s
Array size: 1000,   Time to sort 20M elements: 239.7s vs 242.2s
Array size: 100000, Time to sort 20M elements: 428.4s vs 428.3s
---------------------------------------------------------------
Total:              Time to sort 60M elements: 742.3s vs 740.9s

Variant sorting (mix of ints, strings, and a couple node types):
Array size: 10,     Time to sort 10M elements: 104.9s vs 104.6s
Array size: 1000,   Time to sort 10M elements: 314.5s vs 312.7s
Array size: 100000, Time to sort 10M elements: 514.4s vs 516.1s
---------------------------------------------------------------
Total:              Time to sort 30M elements: 933.8s vs 933.4s

GDScript int sorting:
Array size: 10,     Time to sort 20M elements:  37.4s vs  37.8s
Array size: 1000,   Time to sort 20M elements: 127.2s vs 128.1s
Array size: 100000, Time to sort 20M elements: 217.5s vs 212.1s
---------------------------------------------------------------
Total:              Time to sort 60M elements: 382.1s vs 378.0s

CPPBenchmark int sorting:
Array size: 10,     Time to sort 4B elements:   32.8s vs  32.7s
Array size: 1000,   Time to sort 4B elements:  127.8s vs 128.6s
Array size: 100000, Time to sort 4B elements:  207.3s vs 205.2s
---------------------------------------------------------------
Total:              Time to sort 12B elements: 367.9s vs 366.5s
```

I think the non-CPPBenchmark ones are probably dominated by the GDScript comparison functions, so the CPPBenchmark might be the only one of real value, and even after 12 minutes of interleaved sorting for the two they're basically even.
The slight edge for without across the board may just be random variance, it's a narrow edge, but there doesn't seem to be much reason not to do it, either, it isn't easily detectably worse for raw C++ int arrays, which seems like the worst case.
